Universities teach the equations. Fabs need tool intuition, recipe logic, troubleshooting instinct — and the statistics to prove your process is under control.

ENTER THE CHAMBER

STEP ONE · THE PLASMA

Make the plasma

A negative voltage drives electrons through argon gas until they knock electrons off the atoms. What's left glows between target and wafer: positive argon ions and free electrons.

ARGON → IONS + ELECTRONS

TARGET ATOMS
MOMENTUM TRANSFER
Ar+

STEP TWO · THE IMPACT

Knock atoms off the target

Argon ions arrive with hundreds of electronvolts and hit like a cue ball on a tight rack — each frees one to three surface atoms. Momentum, not heat.

SPUTTER YIELD = ATOMS OUT PER ION IN

STEP THREE · TRANSPORT

Atoms fly to the wafer

Sputtered atoms cross the chamber and rain down onto the substrate below.

STEP FOUR · NUCLEATION

They land and skate

An atom that lands does not stay where it hits — it skates across the surface until it meets another.

STEP FOUR · ISLANDS

Islands form

Two atoms together form a small island. The islands grow as more atoms arrive.

STEP FOUR · THE FILM

The film closes

When the islands finally touch, you have a continuous film. Thickness, uniformity and stress are decided in these seconds.

ALD · DOSE

One layer at a time

Precursor molecules flow in and bond to every open site on the surface.

ALD · SATURATE

The reaction stops itself

Once every site is occupied, more precursor changes nothing. Self-limiting growth is atomic-level thickness control no other method matches.

ALD · PURGE

Clear what didn't react

Inert gas sweeps the chamber. Only the chemisorbed monolayer stays. Shorten this step and it becomes CVD — and conformality is gone.

PLASMA ETCH · IGNITE

Then you take it away

The coil ignites. Ions accelerate across the sheath and strike the masked film.

PLASMA ETCH · CARVE

Cut the trench

Material is removed line by line — the stack opens up, layer by layer.

PLASMA ETCH · DEEP

Straight down

Directional ions carve vertical trenches. Seven knobs decide whether the profile is straight — or ruined.

PLASMA ETCH · PROFILE

Prove the sidewall

A clean SEM cross-section: sharp corners, smooth vertical walls, anisotropy you can defend.

RIE · ICP-RIE · DRIE · ALE

STEP FIVE · METROLOGY

Then you prove it worked

Ellipsometry, XRR, AFM, SEM. Measuring what you made — and knowing when the measurement, not the process, is the thing that's wrong.

  • Cpk is 1.02. Explain to management what that means and what you'll do.

04 — CAREER TRENDS

What fabs are hiring for, and what actually moves you up.

Job titles change between companies. The underlying skills do not. These capabilities appear again and again in process-engineering interviews, promotion cases and transfers.

05 — USE THIS TODAY

Six things that change how you're seen as an engineer.

Nothing to sign up for. These are the habits that separate people who get promoted from people who get overlooked — in interviews and on the floor.

01

Answer with mechanism, not memory

“Pressure affects step coverage” is a fact. “Higher pressure shortens the mean free path, so arriving atoms scatter more and lose directionality — improving sidewall coverage but hurting fill” is understanding. Interviewers hear the difference immediately.

02

Never say “it stopped working”

Say what changed, when, and what stayed constant. Every strong diagnosis starts by separating the variables that moved from the ones that didn't. This one habit makes you sound five years more experienced.

03

Learn to defend a number

If you report 42.3 nm, be ready for “how do you know?” Know your measurement uncertainty, your sampling plan, and whether the tool was calibrated. Engineers who can't defend their data don't get trusted with decisions.

04

One variable at a time is a beginner's rule

It's how you start, not how you finish. Designing a small factorial experiment — three or four factors at once — turns a month of guessing into a week of answers, and it's the most visible upgrade in how you work.

05

Write the failure down

Keep a private log of every problem you solved: symptom, hypothesis, test, result. Two years of that log is your interview material, your promotion case, and eventually the reason others come to you first.

06

Translate up, not down

Your manager doesn't need the chemistry. They need cost, risk and time. “Cpk went from 1.02 to 1.41, so we can drop the extra inspection step” is a sentence that gets budgets approved and names remembered.

The five-step troubleshooting loopUSE IT IN INTERVIEWS. USE IT AT THE TOOL.

  1. 01Observewhat exactly changed
  2. 02Splittool, process or metrology
  3. 03Hypothesisea mechanism, not a guess
  4. 04Discriminateone test, two outcomes
  5. 05Verify & lockprove it, then document

Step 04 is where most people fail. A good test is one whose result rules something out whichever way it goes. If both outcomes leave you equally confused, it isn't an experiment — it's a hope.
